newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia Metals - China seen paying bill for zinc losses.
newsitem.headline: Asia Metals - China seen paying bill for zinc losses.

text.p: China's government could be forced to pick up the potentially large losses of a Chinese zinc producer which must cover its short positions as the market powers to new seven-year price peaks, dealers said on Friday.

Earlier this year, the Zhuzhou smelter sold forward an estimated 90,000 tonnes of zinc contracts at around US$1,100 a tonne, the China Metals newsletter, published by the official Xinhua news agency, reported on July 17.

The firm will now have to meet its obligations, believed to be due in mid-September, by buying at a time when the spot price of zinc on the London Metal Exchange (LME) is just below $1,600 a tonne, dealers said.
"The government will have to pick up the tab for the losses of Zhuzhou. I'm sure they'll look to the government for help," one dealer told Reuters.
"The question is whether they have the material to deliver. The market does not believe they can deliver the material," a dealer for a metal trading house added.
Officials at Zhuzhou could not be reached for comment.

China Metals said Chinese producers, including Zhuzhou, are short by up to 250,000 tonnes of zinc, which could mean the potential losses on these positions adding up to over $100 million at current prices.
"If they can't find any way out of it, the government will have to bail them out. They don't have too many routes open to them," a trader said.
Far East dealers doubt Zhuzhou can produce enough material for delivery when its positions become due in September, although part of the shortfall may be covered by other Chinese smelters.
China Metals said 40,000 tonnes of zinc has already been borrowed from the central government reserve and reprocessed into zinc of a high enough standard for delivery on the LME.
"If they have to deliver, they'll have to come to the market to buy," a trader said.
The Chinese smelters are also hoping that the zinc market, which is heavily overbought, will undergo a downward price correction before they have to cover their short positions.
Traders said a correction should bring the price of three-month metal on the LME down to between $1,400-$1,500 a tonne and help the smelters trim their losses.
"That's cutting it a bit close though, especially if the market heads the other way," a dealer said.
One dealer speculated that a European trade house holding a large long position in zinc may cut a deal with the Chinese.
"Something may happen there although at this time, it doesn't make sense for them to get out of their long position," he said.
The Chinese are also trying to put pressure on the zinc price by engaging in further sales, dealers said.
"But the price has not come down and I don't think that tactic is successful," one said.
In the other base metal markets in the region, Singapore aluminium premiums remained firm due to the tight stock situation in the city-state, dealers said.
"It's vacation time everywhere, but the stock situation here is still tight. There's not much material around," one said.
The LME's Singapore warehouse held 6,050 tonnes of aluminium by Thursday, down from 15,825 tonnes at the end of April.

Premiums for spot aluminium in Japan eased slightly, but were still quoted at around $90-$95 a tonne CIF Japanese ports. They were also seen at $90-$95 a tonne CIF Pusan in South Korea and in Keelung and Kaoshiung in Taiwan.
Aluminium spot premiums were also quoted at $95-$100 a tonne CIF Jakarta.
Copper premiums firmed slightly after the backwardation on the LME contract eased on Thursday although exchange stocks of the red metal in Singapore reached a year high of 52,200 tonnes.
-- Singapore Newsroom (65-8703305)
